name: Networking Fabric
blurb: InfiniBand, Ethernet, and interconnect topology for training clusters.

items.name: Arista AI networking
items.note: Ethernet switching platforms for AI back-end networks at hyperscalers

items.name: Quantum InfiniBand
items.note: The dominant training-cluster interconnect; the Mellanox acquisition that became NVIDIA's moat beyond the GPU

items.name: NVLink / NVSwitch
items.note: The intra-node and rack-scale GPU fabric; NVL72 puts 72 GPUs in one NVLink domain

items.name: Tomahawk switch silicon
items.note: Merchant Ethernet switch chips (51.2T Tomahawk 5 onward) powering AI clusters that choose Ethernet over InfiniBand

items.name: Ultra Ethernet Consortium
items.note: The industry effort to make Ethernet match InfiniBand for AI workloads; v1.0 specification 2025
items.maker: Linux Foundation members incl. AMD, Broadcom, Cisco, Meta, Microsoft

reading.body:
Networking fabric is the layer that determines whether thousands of GPUs act as one machine or as an expensive collection of bottlenecks, and the five entries here map the two competing paths: InfiniBand and Ethernet.

NVIDIA holds the stronger position across both intra-cluster tiers. Quantum InfiniBand dominates inter-node training traffic, a position secured through the Mellanox acquisition. NVLink and NVSwitch handle the shorter distances, binding up to 72 GPUs into a single domain within a rack. That combination means a cluster operator who wants the tightest GPU-to-GPU bandwidth at every scale tier is drawing on NVIDIA for the fabric as well as the compute.

The Ethernet path is narrower but real. Arista supplies switching platforms to hyperscalers already running Ethernet back-ends. Broadcom's Tomahawk silicon, at 51.2 terabits per second from the fifth generation onward, gives those operators merchant chips rather than proprietary ones. The Ultra Ethernet Consortium, whose v1.0 specification arrived in 2025, is the formal attempt to close the performance gap with InfiniBand for AI workloads, backed by AMD, Broadcom, Cisco, Meta, and Microsoft.

The data covers switching and interconnect hardware only. It says nothing about fiber or optical transceivers, cable plant, or how physical topology choices inside a building interact with power distribution and cooling. Whether Ethernet closes the gap in practice, and how that affects cluster design at scale, is not answerable from what is here.
